qs.q: A 30-year-old woman with a 4 cm endometrioma on the left ovary is undergoing laparoscopy. The surgeon performs a cystectomy. What is the most significant risk associated with this procedure?
o: Recurrence of the endometrioma in remaining ovarian tissue after cystectomy.
Damage to ovarian vessels leading to ischemia and possible loss of function.
Peritoneal infection from spillage of cyst contents during the operation.
Development of adhesions between ovary and nearby pelvic sidewall structures.
Bleeding from the ovarian pedicle that may require surgical ligation.
qs.e: Recurrence is a common complication of endometrioma cystectomy.
qs.s: Weekly Obstetrics and Gynaecology Exam - November 13, 2026 (Section A: MCQs)

qs.q: A pathologist examining a cystectomy specimen notes a rare histological type of bladder cancer characterized by copious mucus production within the urine, arising from a urachal remnant. Which type is this?
qs.e: Adenocarcinoma accounts for under 2% of bladder cancers and is found in exstrophic bladders or urachal remnants, presenting with mucosuria. Urothelial carcinoma produces typical frond-like papillary structures rather than abundant mucus.

qs.q: A 55-year-old man undergoes a radical cystectomy for muscle-invasive bladder cancer and requires an incontinent urinary diversion. What is the standard minimum length of the ileal segment harvested for an ileal conduit?
qs.e: An ileal conduit requires a segment of ileum at least 15 cm from the ileocaecal valve with its mesentery. Shorter segments would not provide adequate length to reach the abdominal wall for a tension-free stoma.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer: Haematuria, TURBT, BCG and Cystectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 60-year-old man with muscle-invasive bladder cancer is unfit for radical cystectomy and receives bladder preservation therapy. What is the standard radiation dose typically combined with cisplatin in this trimodality approach?
qs.e: Bladder preservation uses maximal TURBT plus chemoradiation with cisplatin at about 64 to 66 Gy. Lower doses would fail to achieve adequate local tumour control.
qs.s: Bladder Cancer: Haematuria, TURBT, BCG and Cystectomy: MCQs

qs.q: A 68-year-old man with muscle-invasive bladder cancer is scheduled to receive neoadjuvant chemotherapy prior to radical cystectomy. What is the expected survival benefit of adding neoadjuvant cisplatin-based regimens?
qs.e: Neoadjuvant cisplatin-based chemotherapy (gemcitabine and cisplatin, or MVAC) improves survival by about 5 to 8%. Larger survival margins are seen with definitive surgical management alone rather than the modest incremental gain of neoadjuvant drugs.

ai.title: Ovarian Cystectomy
ai.subject: Surgery
ai.summary: Ovarian cystectomy removes a cyst while preserving ovarian tissue, aiming to relieve symptoms, prevent torsion, and avoid malignancy. It is preferred in reproductive‑age women when safe.

sections.p: Ovarian cystectomy is the surgical removal of an ovarian cyst wall, leaving healthy ovarian tissue intact. Diagnosis is based on ultrasound findings of a cystic ovarian mass, often with Doppler assessment of vascularity.
b: Suspicion of malignancy (solid components, papillary projections)

t.b: Detects cyst size, morphology, and vascularity; a complex cyst raises suspicion for malignancy.
Elevated levels may support malignancy but are nonspecific; normal in most benign cysts.
Assesses blood flow; absent flow may indicate torsion.

sections.p: Staging is relevant only for malignant cysts. Benign cysts are staged by size and complexity; malignant cysts use FIGO staging based on tumour spread.
The majority of ovarian cysts are functional, arising from the follicular or luteal phase. Other common causes include endometriomas, dermoid cysts, and parasitic cysts.

t.b: Rules out gestational trophoblastic disease in a pregnant patient.

sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic or present with pelvic pain, bloating, menstrual irregularity, or acute abdominal pain if torsion occurs.
Investigations focus on characterising the cyst and ruling out malignancy.

t.b: Defines cyst size, septations, solid areas, and Doppler flow.
Elevated levels suggest possible malignancy but are not definitive.
Excludes ectopic pregnancy or gestational trophoblastic disease.

sections.p: Red flags include sudden severe pain, haemodynamic instability, or signs of infection. Complications may be haemorrhage, infection, ovarian failure, or adhesions.
Management is surgical, with laparoscopic cystectomy preferred when feasible. The goal is to excise the cyst wall while preserving ovarian tissue.
b: Pre‑op: optimise haemostasis, ensure availability of blood products
Intra‑op: use bipolar cautery, avoid excessive traction
Post‑op: monitor haemoglobin, pain control, early mobilisation

t.b: Prevent postoperative infection; broad‑spectrum coverage if contamination suspected.
Opioid‑free multimodal approach to reduce ileus risk.
Reduces thromboembolic risk and promotes recovery.

sections.p: Post‑operative follow‑up includes clinical review and ultrasound to assess ovarian reserve and detect recurrence.
b: Counsel on contraception and fertility plans

t.b: Checks for residual cysts or recurrence.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe abdominal pain with haemodynamic instability

faq.q: When is cystectomy preferred over drainage?
faq.a: When the cyst wall is thick, complex, or likely malignant; drainage has high recurrence.

faq.q: Can cystectomy be done in a pregnant patient?
faq.a: Yes, if the cyst threatens viability or causes torsion; laparoscopic approach is safe in the second trimester.

faq.q: What is the risk of infertility after cystectomy?
faq.a: Risk depends on cyst size and surgical technique; preserving healthy tissue minimizes impact on ovarian reserve.

exam: What is the first step in managing a patient with a 6 cm complex ovarian cyst? — Identify malignancy risk, order CA‑125, and plan laparoscopic cystectomy if benign.
How would you differentiate an endometrioma from a dermoid cyst on ultrasound? — Endometrioma shows low‑level internal echoes; dermoid has echogenic foci and shadowing.
What is the most appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis for laparoscopic cystectomy? — Broad‑spectrum coverage (e.g., ampicillin‑sulbactam) to cover gut flora.
Why is early mobilisation important after ovarian cystectomy? — Reduces thromboembolic risk and promotes bowel function.
What is the key factor that determines whether to perform detorsion or oophorectomy in ovarian torsion? — Viability of ovarian tissue; if viable, detorsion and cystectomy are preferred.
Which serum marker is most useful for ruling out germ‑cell tumours in an ovarian cyst? — Alpha‑fetoprotein (AFP).
What complication is most feared if haemorrhage is not recognised early post‑cystectomy? — Hypovolaemic shock.
How does a normal CA‑125 level affect your surgical decision? — It lowers suspicion of malignancy but does not rule it out; imaging and intra‑op assessment remain essential.
